📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tracking the stock price amid Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs and alleged spy scandal.

Tracking the stock price amid Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs and alleged spy scandal.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

“We’ve got this,” Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, mentioned Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip firm’s third quarter earnings call.

In a recent development, by Thursday, the manufacturer’s stock price was hovering at around $150 per share, a nearly 40 percent drop from its all-time high on October 6th, and wiping out a brief post-earnings pop on Tuesday night. Meanwhile, Wall Street was paying up for one of Nvidia’s biggest customers as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut at $111.50 per share — 34 percent higher than expected.

Recent findings suggest that looking at the earnings report numbers alone, Nvidia had a blockbuster quarter. Q3 revenue more than doubled from the same period last year up to total $115.8 billion, driven by data center revenue that was up 110 percent and exceeding Wall Street expectations. Nearly $20 billion in revenue came from the highly anticipated Vera Rubin platform, which shipped during the quarter, becoming the “fastest product ramp in firm history,” Kress told investors.

Industry observers note that “Our momentum is real,” Kress said. “With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade, and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia’s leadership position.”.

But investors are stilltrying to reconcile Nvidia’s stellar recent financial performance and position as a central pillar in the AI economy with serious concerns over its future.

It has been revealed that the firm’s stock has taken a stunning tumble in recent weeks. Fueled first by a broader market sell-off of chip stocks amid concerns about the AI bubble, the stock took another blow following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, according to US intelligence sources cited by The New York Times.

Recent findings suggest that harvey Jones, Nvidia’s newly appointed chairman of the board, told investors on the call Tuesday that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and has already tapped an executive search firm to help find a replacement. Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has led the company ever since — famously without a succession blueprint — has become essentially inseparable from it in the eyes of Wall Street and the media. But while Huang may not be ready to let go, posting on X this week that he’d be “honored” to be reinstated as CEO, Nvidia’s executive suite seems ready to move on.

It has been a tumultuous two and a half weeks for Nvidia.

Sources indicate that on October 29th, The Fresh York Times reported that US intelligence agencies believed Jensen Huang to be the target of a Chinese espionage plot. The report centered on his “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center organization and one of Nvidia’s clients. Nvidia initially contested the report, adding that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang “are not unusual or unexpected.”.

In a recent development, nvidia’s stock seemingly remained unaffected by the reports, at least at first. The share price closed at $213.66 on October 29th, down just 0.8 percent from the previous day. (Julian Barnes, one of the reporters on the story, later commented, “I will confess I was kind of surprised that the world’s initial reaction to our October story was a bit muted.”) The stock closed at a 4 percent drop the next day as the entire Nasdaq fell 2.9 percent, the worst single-day decline since June.

The stock continued to fall through Wednesday, November 4th, the day after the blue wave swept the midterms, stoking fears on Wall Street that the upcoming class of Democratic governors in key states like Texas would slow down data center construction. On Thursday, November 5th, Nvidia’s stock fell 9.2 percent, its largest single-day drop in at least a year. But chip stocks began to recover the next day, and by close on Friday, November 6th, Nvidia was back up 2.8 percent to a share price of $186.64.

Then all hell broke loose. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang sent a organization-wide memo to Nvidia staff in which he apologized for engaging in an extramarital affair. The memo coincided with the opening of an independent investigation by Nvidia’s board into Huang’s alleged misconduct and whether company secrets or national security had been compromised. Huang remarked he would cooperate fully with the investigation. By the opening bell on Monday, November 9th, Nvidia shares had tumbled 7 percent and trading volume surged past its three-month average as investors reacted to the memo. After a brief rebound, the stock continued to oscillate the next day, as more details of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang’s relationship emerged. By the time the market closed on Tuesday, November 10th, Nvidia shares were down to $168.89, nearly 10 percent below the closing price on the last day of 2025.

The stock rebounded slightly on Wednesday, November 11th, as investors prepared for Nvidia’s third quarter earnings call, scheduled for the following Tuesday, November 17th. By Wednesday night, however, shares had plunged yet again as media reports circulated that Nvidia’s board was considering ousting Huang, and other reports emerged detailing a second alleged affair, this time between Huang and an Nvidia employee.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia declared Huang’s departure on the morning of Thursday, November 12th, sending the company’s shares falling nearly 14 percent at the open. It closed at just a 4.3 percent dip. The intraday low of $148.80 per share was its lowest price in a year.

On December 1st, Jensen Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee for transcribed interviews. Nvidia’s general counsel will do the same on December 2nd.

Retail investors have already seized the opportunity to buy the dip. In the first 30 minutes of trading on Thursday, November 12th, retail investors bought $111 million of Nvidia shares in the largest-ever first half-hour of opening for the stock, Bloomberg reported, citing Vanda Research.

Nvidia’s average price target is $232.59, with the lowest estimate at $130 and the highest at $350, according to an analysis of analyst projections over the last three months by Google Finance.

Industry observers note that nearly two-thirds of those analysts issued a “Buy” rating for Nvidia in the last three months. Of those, all 30 reiterated that rating post-earnings.

The stock closed at $145.98 on Thursday, a upcoming 52-week low.

Then again, numbers are the core basis for stock market ratings, and numbers may not be Nvidia’s problem right now. It’s everything else — the leadership vacuum, upcoming congressional testimony, regulatory uncertainty, broader questions about neocloud customer financing and sales to China — that will continue to impact the stock in the coming weeks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that anthropic became a public firm on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.

It has been revealed that at the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for.

Industry observers note that anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company stated that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.

However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.”.

With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting.

Recent findings suggest that $104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously confirmed $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry.

Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest.

Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day.

According to recent reports, 28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the firm. Amazon also now has a massive stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%.

The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab claims.

More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the organization’s need for future capital is still far greater.

It has been revealed that anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet.

Industry observers note that all told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a Newly introduced York City bill.
  • Industry observers note that I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website.
  • Recent findings suggest that amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a Newly introduced York City bill.

Industry observers note that I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website. The message is delivered as a pop-up for consumers of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn’t specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I’m logged into Amazon.

Recent findings suggest that amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses.

Clicking on “Act now” on Amazon’s homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states:.

Right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.

It has been revealed that it’s not unusual for Amazon to take a stance on political matters, and it has publicly opposed the Delivery Protection Act since April. What is upcoming is Amazon using its online marketplace to push a political view. It’s uncommon to see a pop-up about legislation when visiting a shopping website.

It has been revealed that the messaging suggests that Amazon is concerned about the potential impact the proposed law would have on its costs. Besides Amazon, the bill targets any company with last-mile delivery facilities in NYC, like FedEx and DoorDash.

It has been revealed that it also raises questions about the potential impact on shoppers should Amazon expand its use of its e-commerce platform for additional political messaging. The pop-up launched today impacts only NYC residents but sets a precedent for Amazon to sway political views on other issues. Amazon has made similar moves internally, including reportedly using an app for its employees to campaign against unionizing. But the new pop-up shows Amazon extending that strategy directly to its people.

In a recent development, given Amazon’s considerable influence in commerce, other companies could copy its actions. Uber and Lyft have previously done so, CNBC reports.

Industry observers note that finally, there’s the question of whether Amazon is fairly depicting the situations surrounding the bill. Notable supporters of the Delivery Protection Act include NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Amazon division of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. Using a platform with massive reach to communicate only one side of an ongoing debate could lead to misinformation and a skewed public perception.

It has been revealed that the Delivery Protection Act is at the moment stalled in the City Council’s Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection. The last hearing on the bill was in April. A committee vote on whether to advance the act to the full City Council hasn’t been set.

The upcoming program expands on the firm’s other offering to underage passengers, Uber Teens, which launched in 2023 and provides rides to teenagers ages 13 to 17 in select cities.

The pilot program for Uber Kids starts in three US cities for a limited time: Austin, Texas; Nashville, Tennessee; and Madison, Wisconsin. Its expansion will depend on how well it performs in those regions. If successful, Uber Kids could bring a whole newly introduced influx of customers to the app, specifically parents and families needing help getting their kids from point A to point B.

In a recent development, on the surface, it feels like a questionable proposition, given all the potential harms and dangers to young people traveling alone with a stranger. But it seems like Uber took those concerns into account. The rideshare app has added a slew of mandatory requirements for both approved guardians and qualified drivers.

According to recent reports, first off, kids won’t simply be able to order a ride for themselves. The adult user must add the child to their family profile and complete an onboarding session covering the service’s safety features. They’ll also need to set up PIN verification for every trip. The parent or guardian must be present at the pickup location and provide the driver with a note containing the drop-off instructions.

Industry observers note that as any parent would likely wonder (myself included), what about the drivers? How are they vetted?

According to Uber, only the highest-rated drivers will be invited to take part in the program. They’ll need to pass thorough background checks and successfully complete an Uber Kids education curriculum. Moreover, they must agree to use live video streaming in their cars so that parents and guardians can watch the trip every step of the way.

It has been revealed that live videos of underage passengers bring up a bunch of potential red flags, but Uber states all recordings will be encrypted, and no driver will have access to the content. Furthermore, sensors and GPS data will track the ride if the trip is interrupted or veers off course.

According to recent reports, uber could face a tough time recruiting drivers for Uber Kids. Transporting minors adds extra responsibility and requires specific skills that many drivers may want to avoid. To sweeten the deal, Uber is offering eligible drivers a $20 bonus on their first ride and an extra $7 per trip after that.

An Uber spokesperson didn’t immediately reply to our request for comment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of people — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.

The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting indicates. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”.

The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.”.

TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response.

Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have released such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the latest John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.

Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the firm is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers.

Industry observers note that the outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging customers from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”.

Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.”.

In a recent development, grand Theft Auto VI is finally here. The launch day for the highly anticipated video game has arrived, more than 13 years after its predecessor.

If you patiently waited more than a decade for GTA 6, you're probably hoping for a long, immersive experience that makes it worth the wait.

In a recent development, good news! Reports are now coming in from game reviewers, and it seems like you're in for a treat. You'll likely be playing GTA 6 for a long time.

Recent findings suggest that an early report from Insider Gaming suggested GTA 6 will take around 50 hours to complete the main campaign. Now that the wider review embargo has lifted, we can get an even more nuanced idea of how long it will take to finish the 91 main story missions GTA 6 has to offer.

For example, our friends at IGN polled four different players who had finished the game, and each of them had something different to say. One player finished the story in "just" 42 hours, which was the lowest estimate. Another took 65 hours, and then a third took 72 hours. Finally, IGN reviewer Luke Reilly said he needed a whopping 115 hours to complete the game.

To be clear, those figures represent the amount of time it took each writer to complete GTA 6's main campaign. If you want to fully complete everything in the game, you're looking at a much longer gameplay time. Much longer.

Sources indicate that aside from GTA 6's main campaign, there are also side quests and an array of interactions, events, and locations to explore. Gamers will likely want to unlock the reported 55 achievements, including the Platinum Trophy and the Mythic achievement.

If you want to do all of that, you could be looking at potentially at least 200 hours of gameplay for GTA 6.

That's not even counting any time spent just wandering the streets of Vice City or cruising around in a car while listening to the stacked GTA 6 soundtrack and radio stations.

In a recent development, so, lock in, gamers (and please take plenty of breaks). More than 200 hours of GTA 6 await. #1969. GTA 6 fans are flying planes into buildings (or trying to)

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

GTA 6 fans are flying planes into buildings (or trying to)

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) debuted on Nov.
  • The Grand Theft Auto series generally revels in grand theft auto, grand theft aerial, and wanton urban destruction.
  • Sources indicate that in GTA 6's predecessor GTA 5, ramming an aircraft into a building would damage the plane and often cause it to explode, with Los Santos' indestructible highrises left intact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) debuted on Nov. 19, prompting gamers everywhere to take the day off and indulge in a lawless land of hedonism and crime. Unsurprisingly, one of the first activities some people tried in the open world sandbox game was to fly a plane into a building. However, these antics haven't been producing the results many expected.

The Grand Theft Auto series generally revels in grand theft auto, grand theft aerial, and wanton urban destruction. Even so, there is particular sensitivity around the subject of crashing planes into buildings. The 9/11 attacks 25 years ago remain a pivotal moment in the U.S. consciousness, to such an extent that many people's minds immediately venture there when presented with a plane and a building.

Sources indicate that in GTA 6's predecessor GTA 5, ramming an aircraft into a building would damage the plane and often cause it to explode, with Los Santos' indestructible highrises left intact. Previous Grand Theft Auto games also didn't allow planes to damage buildings. Nevertheless, some fans wondered if GTA 6 would skew this trend, particularly as it aims to feel realistic.

In a recent development, according to early gameplay clips, this doesn't seem to be the case. In a widely circulated clip by Twitch streamer Windpress, his character parachutes from a plane aimed at a building, only to watch the aircraft apparently pass harmlessly through it. Another popular GTA 6 gameplay video from @DiegoPalmaX revealed a manned plane collide with a building but remain completely intact, slowly falling to the ground and even hitting another structure on the way down.

Such clips have drawn criticism from some Grand Theft Auto fans, who have commented on the lack of realism.

"you can't commit 9/11 in gta 6…" wrote X user @eveisthebastard. "'realism' smh…".

"people will undoubtably say stuff like this doesnt really matter and i would usually agree but when literally all the hype for this game has been 'wow look at all the details there are ten trillion things being simulated' then yeah it really does matter," stated @fbq_2.

Meanwhile, others have argued that it's reasonable for developer Rockstar Games to prevent players from recreating the 9/11 attacks.

"[The point of the game] is to commit crimes. Not be a terrorist," wrote @_MiisterJ. "Why would a game let you recreate 9/11?... Out of everything the game has to offer you draw the line at doing 9/11??".

Sources indicate that some have suggested that GTA 6's unusual interactions between planes and buildings may be the result of bugs. Launch day bugs are common in upcoming video games, with developers often issuing patches to fix them later on. Considering the strange behaviour of GTA 6's planes, particularly when compared to GTA 5, the idea that these are errors seems like a reasonable theory.

However, other social media customers have attributed the viral videos of pristine planes to a toggle in GTA 6's settings. Found under gameplay settings, GTA 6 includes a Reduced Vehicle Damage toggle which increases the amount of abuse your car or plane can take. Though it hasn't been confirmed that this setting was responsible for the nonsensical plane-building interactions seen in widely spread GTA 6 clips, activating it could theoretically help prevent vehicles from becoming deadly fireballs.

According to recent reports, further GTA 6 gameplay videos have supported suggestions that the viral clips are unusual by capturing more typically expected interactions between buildings and planes. A clip from Twitch streamer ohnePixel reveals his small plane exploding after he flies it into a building, though like in GTA 5 the building itself remains undamaged. Another video shared on X by @muaxh03 shows a plane being destroyed after its left wing hits a building, killing the player character.

Industry observers note that in an interview with Love magazine, Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson stated that GTA 6 attempts to balance realism with immersion, indicating that it may deviate where strict adherence to reality would make the game less fun. Whether this includes declining to realistically depict what happens when a jet flies into a highrise will likely become clearer as more people jump in to play. Whos dead on Yellowjackets? (And how did it happen?)

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1584 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that buzz buzz, Yellowjackets hive!
  • Recent findings suggest that trailers for Season 4 have teased the titular soccer team's return home.
  • But hey, if the off-season has you feeling foggy on which teammates (and rivals) have bit the dust (or been bit up), we've got you covered with a recap of all the deaths in Seasons 1, 2, and 3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that buzz buzz, Yellowjackets hive! Season 4 is upon us, and we're ready to be dragged back into the creepy woods of teen chaos and middle-aged mayhem. The Season 3 finale offered some major moments, including the revelation of the Pit Girl's identity and Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) sending out a distress call to the civilized world.

Recent findings suggest that trailers for Season 4 have teased the titular soccer team's return home. However, if the first three seasons have taught us anything, it's that you can take the girl out of the wilderness, but you can't take the wilderness out of the girl. In both the past and present timelines, Shauna (Sophie Nélisse/Melanie Lynskey), Misty (Samantha Hanratty/Christina Ricci), and Taissa (Jasmin Savoy Brown/Tawny Cypress) are grappling for survival and control, so buckle up for a wild ride.

But hey, if the off-season has you feeling foggy on which teammates (and rivals) have bit the dust (or been bit up), we've got you covered with a recap of all the deaths in Seasons 1, 2, and 3.

And keep an eye on this space — the final season of Yellowjackets is sure to see more folks fall, and we'll be updating this list accordingly.

In a recent development, also, wherever possible, we have images with sliders of before and after. Slide 'em if you can stomach it.

Having just moved up from the junior varsity team, Rachel has the grim distinction of being the first Yellowjacket to die. Like the plane's pilots, she died in the crash, from a laceration to her throat.

Father of Travis and Javi, Coach Bill (Carlos Sanz) died as a result of the plane crash that dropped the team in the Canadian wilderness. He'd fallen out of the plane into a tree. In an added bit of brutality, he died in front of Travis, as the teen boy tried to save him from his painful perch in a tree.

It has been revealed that good Christian girl Laura Lee (Jane Widdop) died a hero. After the team found an intact plane in the wilderness, Laura Lee began reading the manual to figure out how to fly it. She eventually took off with her teddy bear Leonard — and her personal lord and savior Jesus — as her co-pilots. But the plane exploded in the air, killing Laura and the Yellowjackets' chance of sending out a member for help.

The queen bee who couldn't hack it in the cabin, Jackie (Ella Purnell) froze to death while sleeping outside. And then she had the bizarre honor of becoming the first to be eaten by the team.

Travis's younger brother Javi (Luciano Leroux) would also be eaten, though the Yellowjackets weren't directly to blame for his death. While the team was hunting Natalie, Javi offered her a hiding place. But before they could get to safety, he fell through the ice of a frozen lake and died. From there, he was eaten.

In a recent development, despite the best efforts of the team, Shauna's baby was stillborn. This was a sad one.

Remember when Misty made a friend? She and Kristen (who was dubbed Crystal the Pistol by the team) bonded in the wilderness over their shared love of music and Steel Magnolias. They grew close enough that Misty shared her secret about destroying the plane's emergency transmitter, which Kristen — understandably — judged. From there, Misty pushed her off a cliff, and proclaimed the girl "missing.".

Real talk: Ben (Steven Krueger) lived way longer than we expected. The plane crash severely damaged his leg, which Misty then amputated on the spot. And incredibly, he survived possible infection, likely starvation, and the burning down of the cabin. But he couldn't escape the Yellowjackets. In a kangaroo court, they convicted him for the cabin's fiery annihilation (despite Misty's best efforts of a defense), and Taissa was chosen to carry out the execution. However, this was not how Ben died. Instead, he was tortured with crippling violence and deplorable conditions — that is, until Natalie took mercy on him and stabbed him fatally in the heart.

Poor Edwin (Nelson Franklin) just wanted to study frogs with his colleague Hannah (Ashley Sutton) and their guide Kodiak (Joel McHale). But then he stumbled in the Yellowjackets camp as they were feasting on Ben's remains. And, well, Lottie welcomed him with an axe to the head. RIP Edwin.

In a recent development, after Edwin was killed, the Yellowjackets imprisoned his surviving friends like they did Ben. When Kodiak tried to escape, he wasn't ended by the girls but by Hannah, who stabbed him in the eye. This was Hannah's bid to show the girls she could be trusted to keep their secret. And it got her through the rest of Season 3 at least.

Yellowjackets began — to quote Sarah McLachlan — building a mystery by introducing the show with the death of the Pit Girl. Underdressed for the snowy weather, she raced through the woods, pursued by masked figures, and ultimately fell into a pit of spikes, which killed her. Season 3 revealed her identity: Mari Ibarra (Alexa Barajas), a persistent rival of Shauna's. Mari too was eaten.

It has been revealed that how Travis (Andres Soto) died was a big mystery in Season 1, with a real bummer of a reveal. In the present, accidentally hanged himself while attempting to talk to the darkness. Lottie was supposed to save him but had a technical malfunction.

In a recent development, in Season 1, Adam Martin (Peter Gadiot) was a mechanic who was having an affair with Shauna. But when Shauna began to suspect he had betrayed her, she stabbed him to death. His murder was covered up with the help of Misty, Nat, Taissa, and Jeff, because Yellowjackets are ride or die. (Sometimes both!).

Masquerading as a journalist, Jessica Roberts (Rekha Sharma) got on the wrong side of Misty Quigley, who fatally poisoned her with fentanyl-laced cigarettes.

Taisaa's family pet was murdered by Night Taissa. Then, his head was placed on creepy basement altar, which would prove a foreshadowing for Ben's fate.

In Season 2, Detective Kevyn Tan (Alex Wyndham) was put in the awkward position of investigating his former high school classmates as he looked into the disappearance of Adam Martin. When his search led him to Lottie's cult's headquarters, he was felled — not by a Yellowjacket! — but by one of their fans. Specifically, Walter Tattersall (Elijah Wood), a citizen detective who fell for Misty. As the two were talking, Walter subtly poisoned Kevyn with a laced hot cocoa.

Nat (Juliette Lewis) died in the Season 2 finale, and we're still not over it. Of all the survivors, she seemed the one who likely to succeed in escaping their past. Worse yet, she was killed by her friend, Misty.

It was an accident. Misty was trying to kill one of Lottie's cult members, Lisa (Nicole Maines), but Nat intervened by throwing her own body in front of the syringe, which was filled with poison. However, Natalie's story continued in the flashbacks. And yet, that only promised to make her ending sadder.

It has been revealed that who killed Lottie Matthews (Simone Kessell)? Well, to the surprise of many, it wasn't Shauna. It was her daughter, Callie Sadecki (Sarah Desjardins). Sure, Callie and Lottie had bonded, no matter how much that enraged Shauna. But when Callie confronted Lottie about stealing the incriminating DAT tape from the Sadecki home, Lottie began saying cryptic things about how Callie was a child of the Wilderness' darkness. In a rage, Callie reacted by shoving Lottie down the stairs.

Recent findings suggest that taissa's high school paramour (Liv Hewson) rejoined to the fold to reignite their romance and proved a solid teammate (Lauren Ambrose) in the present timeline. But their bliss was punctured by Van's cancer diagnosis, and yet that was not how she died! Hopeful the whatever of the wilderness would save her if she sacrificed someone else, Van tried to kill Melissa (Hilary Swank), a ball-capped Yellowjacket who was long thought dead, but had resurfaced under weird circumstances.

According to recent reports, ultimately, however, Van decided not kill Melissa. And in response, Melissa fatally stabbed her and fled, leaving Taissa to bury Van in an unmarked grave. Naturally, she took the opportunity to cut her lover open and eat her heart.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don't be overwhelmed or waste an hour scrolling through your services to determine what to watch. We've got your back, whatever your mood. Mashable offers watch guides for all of the above, broken down by genre: comedy, thriller, horror, documentary, and animation, among others. But if you're seeking something brand new (or just new to streaming), we've got you covered there, too.

Darius Rucker rose to fame in the '90s as the frontman of the rock band Hootie & the Blowfish. In the 2000s, he went solo, first in R&B, then country music. Now, he looks back on a journey that included fame, fortune, struggles with drugs and alcohol, a marriage that fell apart, and much, much more.

According to recent reports, directed by Jason Bergh, Darius Rucker: They Called Me Hootie promises fans a look into the life and music that's kept its subject rolling for decades, with more to come. — Kristy Puchko, Entertainment Editor.

How to watch: Darius Rucker: They Called Me Hootie is now streaming on Hulu and Disney+.

In a recent development, after seven seasons on Netflix, The Circle seemed like it had its last round. However, fans of the popularity-based competition reality show can catch the series in its new home on Hulu, with Season 8 landing this week on the streamer. This time around, the competitors will be both civilians and celebrities, who will vie for ultimate social dominance in the show's apartment block — whether playing as themselves or catfishing the others.

Recent findings suggest that sadly, the Hulu series will not have Netflix host Michelle Buteau, who hosted all seven seasons of the Netflix series. Instead, creator Tinx aka Christina Najjar will have immaculate shoes to fill as the latest Circle host. — Shannon Connellan, Senior Editor.

How to watch: The Circle is now streaming on Hulu.

It has been revealed that nicolas Cage is John Madden in a film you can either watch or not — it's your life. The Hollywood star leads American Hustle director David O. Russell's sports biopic, which follows Madden's NFL coaching and commentary career through to the development of EA Sports' Madden games. In particular, the film explores his partnership with Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis (Christian Bale) and the team's first ever Super Bowl victory in 1977. There's football history, ample prosthetics, and Cage-style roaring from the sidelines, so there might be something in here for you. — S.C.

Starring: Nicolas Cage, Christian Bale, Kathryn Hahn, Sienna Miller, John Mulaney, and Shane Gillis.

How to watch: Madden is now streaming on Prime Video.

HBO's latest documentary paints a personal portrait of the people behind Never Use Alone, the confidential, anonymous, volunteer-operated hotline for people using drugs by themselves — people who don't have someone in their life they could (or feel they could) call for help in an emergency.

According to recent reports, written and directed by Ricki Stern and Jesse Sweet, the short documentary speaks to people who have used or volunteer for the U.S. National Overdose Response Spotting service, who alert emergency services to caller locations if they stop responding while using. Notably, the Trump administration has been moving from "harm reduction" approaches to drug use, including restricting federal funding to support overdose hotlines. The Hotline encapsulates why these grassroots programs are so vital. — S.C.

How to watch: The Hotline is now streaming on HBO.

Recent findings suggest that the collapse of crypto exchange FTX is one of the biggest stories of the tech world in recent years. Now, it comes to Netflix in The Altruists, inspired by Fresh York Magazine articles by Kevin T. Dugan and Jen Wieczner.

Anthony Boyle plays FTX founder and former CEO Sam Bankman-Fried, while Emmy winner Julia Garner plays Caroline Ellison, CEO of FTX's sister tech giant Alameda Research. The Altruists examines their relationship, as well as their larger journey from idealists trying to change the global financial system to fraudsters accused of stealing billions.* — Belen Edwards, Entertainment Reporter.

Starring: Julia Garner, Anthony Boyle, Alex Lawther, Karan Soni, Naomi Okada, Madison Hu, Matt Rife, and Eugene Young.

How to watch: The Altruists is now streaming on Netflix.

The global obsession with Formula 1 will not hit the brakes anytime soon, nor will the women driving to victory in the sport. In a latest documentary from Disney+, you'll go behind the scenes of the F1 Academy, the all-female Formula 1 racing championship series rolled out in 2023. The film particularly focuses on the 2025 F1 Academy season, following drivers Maya Weug, Doriane Pin, Alisha Palmowski, and Chloe Chambers through the competition, and giving you a look at what it takes to get on the hallowed F1 track. — S.C.

Starring: Maya Weug, Chloe Chambers, Alisha Palmowski, and Doriane Pin.

How to watch: The Pursuit: F1 Academy is now streaming on Disney+.

English comedian Oobah Butler has mastered the art of the prank. In 2017, he created fake restaurant The Shed at Dulwich, which became TripAdvisor's top-rated restaurant in London, all without serving a single meal. That same year, he "bullshitted" his way to the top of Paris fashion week by posing as a designer. Since then, he's created documentaries about infiltrating Amazon and getting funding for business ventures. This week, he releases a five-part HBO and A24 series, Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow.

Throughout the series, Butler sets up scams aimed to target five different topics: wellness, wine, dating apps that use AI, music, and royalty. Based on the trailer, his ideas range from pitching a serum made of children's tears to communicating via remote control butt plug. If you love Nathan Fielder's Nathan for You business propositions but wish they were even more out there, this is the show for you. — B.E.

How to watch: Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow premieres Nov. 22 at 11 p.m. ET on HBO and HBO Max.

Though Gentle Monster explores a dark, difficult subject, Léa Seydoux delivers a commanding performance as a woman facing shocking truths in her own family.

In a recent development, written and directed by Corsage's Marie Kreutzer, the film centres on concert pianist Lucy (Seydoux) — and the film's music, by Camille, is an eclectic pop triumph. Captured with elegance and empathy by director of photography Judith Kaufmann, Lucy's idyllic life with her adoring husband Philip (Laurence Rupp) and young son is shattered when the police (led by an excellent Jella Haase as Detective Elsa Kühn) show up with a search warrant, accusing Phillip of a heinous crime. Forced to reckon with the accusations and view the person she loves through an unthinkable upcoming lens, Lucy will never be the same — and it's within this nuance and emotional complexity that Seydoux thrives. — S.C.

Starring: Léa Seydoux, Jella Haase, Laurence Rupp, Malo Blanchet, Anton Rubtsov, Nils Strunk, Sylvester Groth, Patrycja Ziółkowska, Regina Fritsch, and Catherine Deneuve.

How to watch: Gentle Monster is now streaming on Netflix.

The wrongful conviction of Alfred Chestnut, Andrew Stewart, and Ransom Watkins (the so-called Harlem Park Three) is the focus of HBO's latest documentary, When a Witness Recants.

Directed by Dawn Porter and produced by Ta-Nehisi Coates, the film examines the miscarriage of justice that occurred in Baltimore, Maryland, when the three innocent 16-year-olds were sentenced to life in prison for the murder of 14-year-old DeWitt Duckett in 1983. Featuring interviews with Chestnut, Stewart, and Watkins, the film explores the 36 years they wrongfully spent in prison, the failures of the Baltimore Police Department, and their path to freedom and exoneration in 2019. — S.C.

How to watch: When a Witness Recants is now streaming on HBO Max.

American author Patricia Highsmith wrote a string of sensational thriller novels, but she's best known for created Tom Ripley, the killer con man who's spawned a series of adaptations all his own.

It has been revealed that in A Talent For Murder, however, the Ripley adaptation gets a new, riveting wrinkle. Helen Mirren stars as Highsmith, who's living in a remote cabin in Switzerland when an ambitious young American man (Alden Ehrenreich) comes calling. He wants her to write another Ripley novel, to appease his publisher bosses back in the states. She wants a mind to mess with, and he's seductively willing. While he romances a beguiling young woman (Olivia Cooke), author and admirer join forces to imagine a fictional scenario worth of Ripley. What's fantasy and what's reality? The lines blur in this sexy and wickedly entertaining film. As I cheered in my review out of TIFF, "A Talent For Murder is darkly funny, freshly thrilling, and unrepentantly seductive. It's not a Ripley sequel, but it's damn close." — K.P.

Starring: Helen Mirren, Alden Ehrenreich, and Olivia Cooke.

How to watch: A Talent for Murder is now available for rent or purchase on Prime Video, Apple TV, and Fandango at Home.

Comedy nerds, you have to see this one.

It has been revealed that the full title of this superb documentary from Nick Davis is You Had to Be There: How the Toronto Godspell Ignited the Comedy Revolution, Spread Love & Overalls, and Created a Community That Changed the World (in a Canadian Kind of Way). Its focus is looking back at the 1972 Toronto production of Godspell, which boasted such not-yet-famous performers as Martin Short, Eugene Levy, Gilda Radner, Victor Garber, Andrea Martin, Dave Thomas, Jayne Eastwood, and Paul Shaffer. And most of the above offer interviews, home movies, and personal recordings of this pivotal moment in Canadian comedy.

Recent findings suggest that this movie was one of my absolute favorites at last year's Toronto International Film Festival. And as I cheered in my review, "You Had to Be There gifts audiences plenty of laughs, and so much more. This is not some fluffy celebration of comedians or even Godspell. Davis and firm have come together to craft a documentary that is both informative, historical, entertaining, and deeply humane."* — K.P.

Starring: Martin Short, Eugene Levy, Victor Garber, Andrea Martin, Dave Thomas, Jayne Eastwood, and Paul Shaffer.

How to watch: You Had to Be There is now available for purchase on Apple TV and Fandango at Home.

Industry observers note that directed by John Ripa and Alyce Tzue, Steps is a soft-goth twist on Cinderella. Centered not on on the famous princess (Amanda Seyfried) but her so-called evil stepsister Lilith (Ali Wong), this animated adventure offers a tale of rebellion, regret, sisterhood, and magic. The story you thought you know gets a fun shake-up that includes not only a fairy godmother (Bette Midler) and a charming prince (Daniel Radcliffe), but also a chipper talking frog (Stephanie Hsu), a medieval mean girl (Nikki Glaser), and a hot troll (Young Mazino).

Whether you've got a kiddo who's gotten a little too old for the standard Disney Princess fare, or you can't get enough of fractured fairytales, Steps is sure to please. As I wrote in my review, "Cheers to the small army of writers who've earned screenplay and story-by credits on this film (Ava Tramer, James Madejski, Jen Chuck, Dana Schwartz, Felicia Ho, Riki Lindhome, and Kate Micucci). Steps gives audiences a familiar dose of fairy-tale tropes, then uses them to explore topics that can be tricky to explain to kids... But it's through the conflict of two sisters — one privileged and playing by the rules, the other marginalized and defiant — that each learns how to be better and more loving to themselves and each other. And kindness is contagious." — K.P.

Starring: Ali Wong, Amanda Seyfried, Stephanie Hsu, Nikki Glaser, Daniel Radcliffe, Young Mazino, Peter Dinklage, and Bette Midler.

In a recent development, how to watch: Steps debuts on Netflix on Nov. 20.

In its third season, Percy Jackson and the Olympians moves beyond the ground covered by the movies, giving Rick Riordan fans their first onscreen adaptation of The Titan's Curse. That means it's time to give a warm welcome to Bianca and Nico di Angelo (Olive Abercrombie and Levi Chrisopulos), two fan-favorite characters making their screen debuts this season.

In a recent development, the arrival of Bianca and Nico isn't the only major change shaking up Camp Half-Blood this season. Thalia (Tamara Smart) is back, which means Percy (Walker Scobell) is no longer the only child of the Major Three at camp. As these two embark on a quest to save a kidnapped Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries) and the goddess Artemis (Dafne Keen), will they get along? Or will they turn on one another in a conflict of mythic proportions? Book fans know that The Titan's Curse is where things get dark, so be warned. But don't worry: At least we know we'll be getting dam jokes.* — B.E.

According to recent reports, starring: Walker Scobell, Leah Sava Jeffries, Aryan Simhadri, Dior Goodjohn, Daniel Diemer, Charlie Bushnell, Tamara Smart, Olive Abercrombie, Levi Chrisopulos, Dafne Keen, Saara Chaudry, Ming-Na Wen, Hubert Smielecki, Jesse L. Martin, and Holt McCallany.

It has been revealed that how to watch: Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 3 premieres Nov. 20 on Disney+, with upcoming episodes weekly.

According to recent reports, buzz, buzz! The Yellowjackets are back for their fourth and final season. In past and present timelines, the Yellowjackets are dropping like flies. We can't wait to see how things shake out for Shauna, Misty, Tai, and Melissa. (And Jeff!).

Sources indicate that last season ended with teen Natalie successfully escaping teen Shauna's hunt to use the frog scientist's repaired SAT phone to call for help. But anyone who can count can take a look at the Season 4 trailer and see that not all of residents of Camp Yellowjacket will make it back to civilization. This season we're likely to learn what happened to Hannah and Akilah. But will the show finally reveal the mysteries of the wilderness? What does that symbol mean? And of the still-standing Yellowjackets in the present-day timeline, who'll make it alive to season's end? — K.P.

Starring: Melanie Lynskey, Christina Ricci, Tawny Cypress, Warren Kole, Sarah Desjardins, Hilary Swank, Sophie Nélisse, Sophie Thatcher, Jasmin Savoy Brown, Samantha Hanratty, Courtney Eaton, Liv Hewson, Kevin Alves, Jenna Burgess, and Nia Sondaya.

Industry observers note that how to watch: Yellowjackets Season 4 premieres Nov. 20 on Paramount+.

Thanks to Don Bluth, we have magical and thrilling animated adventures like The Secret of NIMH, The Land Before Time, An American Tail, Anastasia, and All Dogs Go to Heaven. Now, documentarians Dave LaMattina and Chad N. Walker take a look back at this American animator's life and works, with the documentary Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There.

The film ushers audiences back to the early days of Bluth's life as a little boy inspired by Walt Disney's groundbreaking animated feature, Snow White and the Seven Dwarves. Then, through archival footage, clips from a variety of animated films — including Bluth's — and interviews with the man himself, Somewhere Out There charts the dizzying highs and devastating lows that seemed to come with every project. There's a story about payments coming in a paper bag that's sure to have you cracking up. But most of all, it's riveting how candid Bluth is, whether recounting his animation company's rivalry with the Disney studio or his own personal struggles.

A must-see for any true animation lover, Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There is not to be missed. —K.P.

How to watch: Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There is now available on VOD.

#1964. Japan has a word for our dopamine-addicted internet brains: Dopagaki

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1607 w)

Japan has a word for our dopamine-addicted internet brains: Dopagaki

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that forty-five minutes on TikTok can pass in the blink of an eye.
  • In Japan, there's a word for this particular kind of digital restlessness: dopagaki.
  • Roughly translating to "dopamine brat," the Japanese slang term combines dopamine with "gaki," a disparaging word for a child, to describe someone who craves a steady stream of stimulation, whether it's short-form videos, social media, or fast-paced entertainment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that forty-five minutes on TikTok can pass in the blink of an eye. Two minutes watching a video at normal speed? An eternity. Somewhere between scrolling through Instagram Reels, checking our phones during movies, and skipping to the best part of a song, our relationship with entertainment has become a little absurd. We're consuming more of it than ever, yet we seem to have less patience for any individual piece of it.

In Japan, there's a word for this particular kind of digital restlessness: dopagaki.

Roughly translating to "dopamine brat," the Japanese slang term combines dopamine with "gaki," a disparaging word for a child, to describe someone who craves a steady stream of stimulation, whether it's short-form videos, social media, or fast-paced entertainment. But while dopagaki might sound like Japan's answer to the American "iPad kid," its reported origins are a little more surprising. The expression has been linked to a viral post about the structure of a pop song, and some of the young people it appears to mock have started using it to describe themselves.

According to recent reports, so, a word associated with mocking a generation's appetite for instant gratification and excessive screen time has become a self-aware joke about the way we consume media. But dopagaki indicates just as much about the entertainment itself, packaged to deliver one satisfying moment after another, as it does about the people consuming it.

After all, when something new is always just a swipe away, is it any wonder we've grown impatient waiting for it?

According to recent reports, dopagaki (ドパガキ) is an abbreviation of the Japanese phrase "dōpamin chūdoku no gaki," or "dopamine-addicted brat." It describes someone who constantly craves quick bursts of stimulation, whether that's endlessly scrolling through TikTok, playing video games, or skipping ahead in longer videos to get to the good parts. Even platforms like YouTube have made this kind of consumption easier, with features like video chapters that let viewers jump straight to the moments they want to see.

The word itself isn't particularly kind. In Japanese, "gaki" is a dismissive term for a child, closer to "brat" than "kid." And despite the reference to dopamine, dopagaki isn't a medical diagnosis. Dopamine plays a role in motivation, learning, and reward, and enjoying hyperstimulating entertainment doesn't necessarily mean someone is addicted to it.

But the expression's reported origins reveal something interesting about the way we consume that entertainment. It wasn't a TikTok video or a smartphone habit that inspired the term — it was a pop song.

In December 2024, a Japanese user on X described the structure of "Lilac," a song by popular Japanese rock band Mrs. GREEN APPLE, using the phrase "dōpamin chūdoku no gaki." The observation centered on the song's rapid succession of musical payoffs, with catchy melodies and energetic transitions arriving in quick succession. There's barely a moment for the listener to settle into one musical idea before another comes along to capture their attention.

The original post didn't use the shortened form dopagaki, and it's unclear exactly when that abbreviation first appeared. But the musical reference offers an intriguing window into the larger cultural phenomenon. The conversation wasn't simply about people demanding constant stimulation. It was also about entertainment seemingly designed to satisfy that demand.

Industry observers note that and that idea extends well beyond a single pop song. Think about the videos that change shots every few seconds, the rise of microdramas, or the way creators are encouraged to hook viewers in the first three seconds of a video before they've had a chance to scroll away. Each newly introduced moment promises something more exciting than the last. Entertainment isn't just competing for our attention anymore. It's testing our patience.

By the summer of 2026, dopagaki had made its way into Japanese youth slang.

In a recent development, in June, Joshikosei Lab, a Japanese marketing research group focused on teenage girls, included dopagaki among seven trending expressions identified through a survey of 60 high school girls. The group described the term as a humorous, self-deprecating way of acknowledging digital overconsumption, including the habit of watching TikTok while drying your hair or taking a bath.

It's a small survey, not a definitive measure of how widely the term is used. Still, it points to an interesting development: Some of the young people who might otherwise be the targets of the insult are now using it to laugh at themselves.

Industry observers note that that doesn't mean dopagaki has lost its derogatory edge. Calling someone else a dopamine-addicted brat can still sound condescending, particularly when it's used to dismiss their tastes or suggest that an entire generation has lost the ability to concentrate. But describing yourself as dopagaki is something different. It's a way of recognizing your own habits, perhaps with a little embarrassment, and finding humor in how familiar they've become.

It's also a distinctly internet-native way of processing a shared anxiety. Rather than having a serious conversation about digital dependency every time someone finds themselves scrolling past midnight, there's now a word that captures the experience in five Japanese characters.

Sources indicate that and apparently, the joke resonates. In a separate October survey of 94 Japanese high school girls, 16 percent named dopagaki as their most-used slang expression of 2026, while another 17 percent stated they'd encountered the term on social media but didn't use it themselves. The findings suggest that the expression has gained some recognition among young people, even if not everyone identifies with it.

Sources indicate that perhaps that's part of what makes dopagaki such a revealing piece of internet slang. It captures both the humor and the discomfort of recognizing our own habits in a culture that rarely gives us a reason to put our phones down.

American internet culture has developed its own vocabulary for our increasingly complicated relationship with screens.

There's the "iPad kid," a typically unflattering description of children raised with tablets seemingly glued to their hands. As Know Your Meme documents, the term gained traction on TikTok through videos mocking children so absorbed in their screens that they appear oblivious to the world around them. Then there's "brainrot," a term that's become both a criticism of mindless online consumption and an affectionate description of the absurd content people can't stop watching.

Dopagaki exists somewhere between the two. Like "iPad kid," it can carry a generational judgment, implying that young people have become dependent on screens and instant gratification. Like "brainrot," it can also function as a self-aware joke, a way of admitting that your own relationship with the internet might be a little excessive.

Industry observers note that but there's an crucial distinction. The iPad kid is often someone else's child, usually invoked as an example of what's wrong with the next generation. Dopagaki, at least in its more playful usage, can be a label people willingly apply to themselves. And the habits it describes hardly belong to one generation.

Adults scroll through TikTok during commercial breaks, check notifications in the middle of conversations, and watch television with a second screen in their hands. The same people who complain about children needing constant entertainment may struggle to get through a quiet moment without reaching for their own phones.

Industry observers note that according to DataReportal's Digital 2027 Global Overview Report, which draws on research conducted in 2026, online adults spend an average of 19 hours and 18 minutes per week using social media and online video platforms. That's more than two and a half hours a day on average spent watching, scrolling, and consuming content.

Of course, there's nothing inherently wrong with enjoying short videos, high-energy music, or entertainment that gets straight to the point. The more interesting question is how much of our appetite for constant stimulation comes from personal habit, and how much is shaped by the digital environments we've built around ourselves.

Social platforms are designed to keep us watching, listening, and scrolling. Creators work within those systems, learning to capture attention swiftly and hold onto it for as long as possible. Audiences, in turn, grow accustomed to an internet where the next entertaining thing is always a swipe away. Our habits shape the content we consume, and that content shapes our expectations of what entertainment should deliver.

Which brings us back to dopagaki. What was used in one early post to describe the structure of a pop song has become a way to capture a much broader experience of living online. There's something fitting about young people turning that criticism into a joke, particularly when the adults judging their screen habits are often just as attached to their own devices.

#1953. Heated Rivalry 4DX is fun, but how does it compare to Wicker 4DX?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2139 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Heated Rivalry 4DX is fun, but how does it compare to Wicker 4DX?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2139 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I heard about Wicker 4DX, it seemed a cheeky joke.
  • In my review of Wicker 4DX, I detailed how the motion-enhanced theaters "vibrated and bucked, yes, in rhythm with the Wicker Husband's thrusting." After the first love scene, the elated audience applauded and cheered.
  • So, my hopes were high when it was declared Heated Rivalry would follow in Wicked's bouncy footsteps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I heard about Wicker 4DX, it seemed a cheeky joke. Praise was fervent for the fantasy romance that stars Olivia Colman as a lonely Fisherwoman who weds a Wicker Husband (Alexander Skarsgård). Admittedly, I was invested at "Olivia Colman." But buzz around the spirited sex scenes suggested Wicker 4DX would be a rollicking good time. So, naturally, as a journalist, it was my job to find out.

In my review of Wicker 4DX, I detailed how the motion-enhanced theaters "vibrated and bucked, yes, in rhythm with the Wicker Husband's thrusting." After the first love scene, the elated audience applauded and cheered. It was great fun, but also a cinematic experience that fostered a sense of community among romance fans who don't want to hide their horniness. Here was a safe space to giggle and swoon without fear of judgment. It reminded me of the gleeful days of slumber parties, and what a treasure they were.

So, my hopes were high when it was declared Heated Rivalry would follow in Wicked's bouncy footsteps.

Recent findings suggest that the Canadian phenomenon went from streaming to theaters, playing two episodes at a clip for fans to rewatch together. Then, it was confirmed that episodes 5 and 6 would be getting the 4DX treatment. As Mashable's newly minted 4DX-pert, I was obliged to go.

Sources indicate that so, how did Heated Rivalry 4DX compare the Wicker 4DX? Let's get into it.

Recent findings suggest that I can hear you gasping. But think about it! This isn't the early days of the forbidden romance between hockey rivals Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie). What played in 4DX were the episodes "I'll Believe in Anything" and "The Cottage.".

This means the screening began with the awkward morning after another fumbled hook-up between Shane and Rose Landry (Sophie Nélisse). This episode is the one where they break up, and from there, where flirtations and hand-holding suggest the intimacy between Shane and Ilya is blossoming into a love neither can admit to. That is, until Ilya does say "I love you," over the phone, in a far-away tunnel in Russia (and in Russian).

In a recent development, episode 5 is full of beautiful dramatic moments, including Scott Hunter (François Arnaud) celebrating his championship win by bringing his lover Kip (Robbie G.K.) onto the ice, and coming out publicly. But there aren't many lusty moments. So, the 4DX seats would tease the audience by thrumming in sync with the show's soundtrack or vibrating anytime a text message arrived.

Sources indicate that episode 6 finally offers some fooling around in Shane's bedroom and then the oral sex scene, where Ilya goes down on Shane as he takes a call from Hayden (Callan Potter). Fans hooted and laughed as the seats attempted to match the rhythm of Ilya's motions. But it doesn't compare to the rocking of Wicker, which offered multiple sex scenes. The first of them is on the wedding night between the Fisherwoman and the Wicker Husband, and the motion added was so thoughtfully rendered in seat-rocking that the audience cheered upon its climax.

Heated Rivalry 4DX cannot compete here, or rather, it doesn't, by focusing on the final two episodes.

Industry observers note that well, for one thing, the violence hits harder. After the funeral for Ilya's father, he gets into a physical confrontation with his brother Alexei (Slavic Rogozine), who thrusts the hockey star into a wall. Ilya responds in kind, and the audience gasped as our bodies were collectively slammed in the comfort of our seats.

Likewise, the brief hockey scenes has a fresh sense of immersion. In slo-mo scenes, the seats slowly but smoothly rocked from side to side, mimicking the motion of the players' hips as they skated. And as "I'll Believe in Anything" is the episode where Shane "gets [his] bell rung," that hit is hard. But not so hard you'll get a concussion.

Of course, 4DX is more than just shimmying seats. Some charming elements included fog emitting from the front of the theater while Shane grills (too many) burgers at the cottage. Or, when Ilya is playing in the hotel pool with children or splashing in the lake near the cottage, a spritz of water was emitted. The aim seemed to be off for me and my guest, as we could see the water rise and hiss of the propulsion, but we never actually got wet, or even misted. A mist opportunity, then?

And speaking of missed opportunities, I was actually disappointed that 4DX didn't use snow.

It's an element that I saw in Wicker 4DX and was quite awed by. And it might have been mindfully employed in the tunnel scene, as snow falls in the distance as Ilya pours his heart out over the phone. In this scene, 4DX did offer a slight breeze, which was a little chilly and did enhance the experience, making it feel more like we were out in the night with this lonely lover. But snow would have been a marvelous touch.

That's not something I thought I'd ever write. But here we are.

In Wicker, I was wowed by the smell of a wet forest and of fire catching. In Heated Rivalry, I could smell the chlorine of the pool in the aforementioned hotel scene and the scent of an ice rink in the arena sequences. I could hear the hiss of the machine that emits odor throughout the two episodes. But whether it was a beach scene, the burger grilling scene, or lakeside, I couldn't smell anything but a vaguely chemical smell.

I even thought perhaps own nose was the issue, perhaps stuffy from the radical weather changes that have been hitting Upcoming York City. My sniff test was putting my bottled ice tea under my nose, but I could make out the earthy smell of the tea and the hint of lemon, and even the whiff of my perfume as my wrist raised near my nose. So, not human error!

For the sake of science, I did attend the exact same 4DX theater as I did for Wicker, though this time my seats were in the last row instead of near the front. This shouldn't have impacted the smells or splashing though. And it did have one major drawback.

Recent findings suggest that online fans of this series have ranged from enthusiastic to feral. In person, it's similarly a mixed bag. Walking into the theater, I immediately clocked fans wearing Heated Rivalry merch, like T-shirts with Shane and/or Ilya on them, jerseys with the fictional hockey teams logos, and a ball cap embroidered with "I'm coming to the cottage.".

Like with Wicker DX, the energy was joyful and excited. People chatted and snacked. And I was surprised that the theater was not totally packed. But as the trailers started, more people came in. The seats slowly filled, some with fans loaded down with snacks. I will admit, my earlier 4DX experience informed our behavior here. My guest and I did buy snacks: chicken tenders, fries, and hot dogs with drinks. But we also got to the theater early enough to eat before the 4DX of it all kicked off. I'd remembered it being tricky to even eat popcorn in Wicker 4DX, in part because I'd not seen the movie before and so could not predict when my seat might buck.

Shout-out to the poor fellow to my left. He sat down during the trailers, unaware that some trailers have motion-activated moments in 4DX. As our seats bobbed up and down unexpectedly during a trailer for Disney's Hexed, I heard him gasp. I turned just in time to see the nachos leap up from their cardboard tray and into the open bag on his lap. "Oh, come on!" he yelped in righteous dismay. He was a gentleman, and tended to this snack-tastrophe as quietly as could be expected. So, this is less a scolding and more a warning: Choose your snacks and timing wisely in 4DX.

It has been revealed that the others around me were far less mindful of others. Two women to our right talked the whole time, as if they were watching at home. Yes, they even chattered while Shane maps out their whole could-be life together in bed at the cottage. Then there was the gaggle of women who collectively left together (presumably to re-snack or use the bathroom) and made a ruckus as they went, and then used flashlights when they got back to locate something misplaced in the shuffle. Lastly, there was the woman in front of me, who kept recording the screen with her phone.

Look, I'm no fan of using phones in a theater. For one, it's a place of immersion, where we are meant to shut out the outside world. For another, it's a place of community. However slick you think you're being, you absolutely are disturbing those around you when you pull out a device that is essentially a beam of light in a dark room.

In a recent development, but hey, I realize 4DX is a less serious cinematic experience. It's basically movie meets ride. And so I did expect to see some phones pop up for bits of the screening, as I'd seen plenty of POV videos from Wicker 4DX's run. However, this Heated Rivalry fan was recording her clips and then logging into Instagram to post immediately after. Plus, her brightness was SO high that I could tell you her name, or at least her Insta handle.

In a recent development, behavior like this disrupts other people's immersion into what they paid to see. While the recorder might be looking to build online community (or cachet) through the clips, they're essentially ignoring those around them in favor of this aim. It's sacrificing not only the recorder's ability to live in the moment of the movie (or show) but also others, without their okay.

Still, despite these anti-social choices, there were moments of glorious fan unity in Heated Rivalry 4DX. When Wolf Parade's song "I'll Believe in Anything" began to play, there was a frisson in the air that had nothing to do with pipes, odors, or shaking seats. The theater was silent as we all watched and pined for the happy ending we know by heart by now. As Kip took to the ice, I could hear choked gasps of anticipation. When Scott kisses him, there were cheers and applause. Then, when Ilya says the line ("I'm coming to the cottage"), the audience roared with excitement as if we'd won the Stanley Cup. Plus, they were chirps and cheers throughout the final sequence of episode 6, where Shane comes out to his parents and Ilya uses the word "boyfriend" for the first time.

In those moments, it was a pleasure to be in that crowd. And yet, it was easier to enjoy Wicker.

Industry observers note that I can't be certain, but I could guess based on release dates that fewer people in the Wicker 4DX had seen the production before their showtime than was true of Heated Rivalry. The most ardent loons I know have seen the Crave series top to bottom five or six times. And perhaps that means that rather than coming for a whole experience, these 4DX attendees were coming for massive emotional moments. Those don't really translate into big physical motions.

While this is a streaming drama series that does a lot of things beautifully, it's stretches of earnest dialogue don't make for the kind of unserious fun the romantic comedy of Wicker allowed for. Still, it was a fun night out to relish in a show I love with friends and fellow fans.

In a recent development, my advice to you, should more showtimes be added, would be if you go to Heated Rivalry 4DX, zip your lip and put your phone away. And look, if you do blueprint to pull out your phone, at least have enough consideration for your fellow audience member to do it with the brightness down, and maybe not smack dab in the middle of the theater. Don't make your short attention span or craving for content cachet someone else's problem.

#1950. Latest Update: Scientists found a star inside of another giant star

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (923 w)

Latest Update: Scientists found a star inside of another giant star

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers have detected a star slightly less massive than the sun inside a giant star for the first time.
  • It has been revealed that the two stars, in the nearby Andromeda Galaxy, had circled each other for thousands of years.
  • According to recent reports, scientists think the same kind of spiral explains how many star pairs end up circling each other very closely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers have detected a star slightly less massive than the sun inside a giant star for the first time.

It has been revealed that the two stars, in the nearby Andromeda Galaxy, had circled each other for thousands of years. Then the giant swallowed the smaller star. The trapped star took only about seven years to spiral to the center, where the two merged into a single star. NASA's James Webb Space Telescope supplied the final evidence.

According to recent reports, scientists think the same kind of spiral explains how many star pairs end up circling each other very closely. In this case, the small star didn't survive. But in other pairs, the giant's gas gets blasted away first, leaving both stars in an orbit that takes just hours or days instead of years. Those tight pairs can later become black holes or super-dense dead star cores called neutron stars, or explode as supernovas. Some also send out gravitational waves, which are ripples in space and time.

Lead author Viraj Karambelkar, a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University, and an international team reported the discovery Wednesday in the journal Nature.

The researchers nicknamed the larger star "Big Bao," and it earned the name. It had about seven times the sun's mass and 350 times its width, shining 18,000 times brighter.

"It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data," mentioned Karel Temmink, a doctoral student at Radboud University in the Netherlands, in a statement.

Its partner, "Little Bao," had about 70 percent of the sun's mass.

Sources indicate that stars like Significant Bao swell up near the end of their lives. If our sun did the same, it could grow past Earth's orbit. As Big Bao swelled, Little Bao began skimming its outer layer and stripping away gas. Soon the small star was orbiting inside the giant. The gas there was spread so thin that Little Bao stayed intact for years, according to the paper. Still, the gas slowed it down, much like air slows a thrown ball, until it eventually sank toward the giant's core.

No telescope can literally see inside a star. But friction from the small star's plunge churned the giant's gas and carried that heat to the surface. There it showed up as seven years of steady brightening. When the team compared the starlight from before and after the eruption — and tested computer models against it — the best explanation was a small star spiraling inside the giant.

According to recent reports, when the smaller one finally reached the giant core, gravity likely ripped it apart. That triggered a blast that hurled about one-tenth of the giant's outer material into space.

Their encounter was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," said Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia.

It has been revealed that the explosion itself came on surprisingly fast. The team thought an outburst would take years. Instead, it took just a week from when its brightness started rising to its peak, said Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain.

Scientists expect many star pairs to go through this phase, but catching one in the act has taken incredible luck.

"The timescales involved are short, months to years, and the rates at which they form are low," astrophysicist Jason Nordhaus wrote in a commentary published alongside the study. "Just a few stars exist in this phase at any given time in a galaxy such as the Milky Way.".

Recent findings suggest that astronomers usually piece together star mergers long after they happen. This time, a fleet of telescopes followed Bao as the events unfolded. The team first noticed the star acting strangely in Feb. 2023, in data from NASA's now-retired NEOWISE mission. In Sep. 2024, another telescope saw it brightening and puffing out dust. In July 2025, NASA's Spherex telescope happened to catch it fading in visible light while it brightened in infrared light. Then, on Oct. 17, 2025, the Zwicky Transient Facility, a sky-scanning telescope in California, spotted the eruption.

Webb took its look on Dec. 24, 2025, just 47 days after the eruption peaked. No telescope had ever followed up on an event like this so quickly, Karambelkar noted.

It has been revealed that what the newly single star, now just called "Bao," will become remains an open question. Only future observations will show how it settles down.

NASA's new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Vera Rubin Observatory in Chile will scan huge areas of sky over and over. They should spot events like this in hundreds of nearby galaxies.

"There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead," Karambelkar said.
